nameStory: The yellow buckeye gets its name from its bright yellow flowers that bloom in spring, distinguishing it from its red-flowered cousins. The 'buckeye' part comes from the large, glossy brown seeds that have a lighter patch resembling the eye of a deer or buck. Native Americans and early settlers thought these seeds looked remarkably like the alert, watchful eye of a white-tailed deer.
description: Yellow buckeye is a magnificent deciduous tree that can tower 65 to 150 feet tall, making it one of the tallest trees in eastern forests. It has distinctive palmate leaves that look like an open hand with 5-7 leaflets radiating from a central point. In spring, it produces showy clusters of yellow flowers that stand upright like candles, followed by large, leathery seed pods containing glossy brown buckeye seeds. This stately tree has smooth, gray bark and creates an impressive canopy in mature forests.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large palmate leaves with 5-7 leaflets arranged like fingers on a hand, each leaflet 4-6 inches long with fine teeth along the edges. The leaflets feel smooth and thin, turning golden-yellow in fall.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Upright clusters of creamy-yellow flowers bloom in late spring, each cluster 4-6 inches tall and shaped like a cone or candle. Individual flowers are small but numerous, creating a showy display.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Large, round to oval seeds (buckeyes) are glossy chocolate-brown with a lighter tan patch, about 1-2 inches across. They're contained in smooth, leathery capsules that split open in fall.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth, light gray bark on young trees becomes slightly furrowed with age but remains relatively smooth compared to other large trees. It feels firm but not deeply ridged.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as a tall, straight tree with a rounded crown, often reaching impressive heights in rich forest soils. Branches are opposite each other and relatively thick.

habitat: Yellow buckeye is extremely rare in New England, with only a handful of planted specimens documented. In its native range, it thrives in rich, moist soils of mountain slopes and river valleys, typically in mixed hardwood forests. Any yellow buckeyes found in New England would likely be in arboretums, botanical gardens, or as rare landscape plantings in protected, well-watered locations.

seasonality.spring: Large palmate leaves emerge in mid to late spring, followed by spectacular upright clusters of yellow flowers that bloom for several weeks. The fresh green leaves and bright flowers make identification easiest in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Full leafy canopy provides dense shade, with the distinctive hand-shaped leaves being the primary identifying feature. Developing seed pods begin to form after flowers fade.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn brilliant golden-yellow before dropping, and the large, glossy buckeye seeds fall from split-open pods. The seeds are very distinctive and make great identification aids.
seasonality.winter: Large, sticky winter buds are arranged opposite each other on thick twigs. The smooth gray bark and massive size help identify this tree even without leaves.

funFact: Yellow buckeye seeds are mildly toxic to humans but were traditionally processed by Native Americans into a nutritious flour by crushing and leaching them multiple times in water to remove the bitter compounds - essentially detoxifying them through careful preparation.
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with horse-chestnut, which also has palmate leaves and similar flowers, but horse-chestnut has white flowers with pink markings rather than yellow, and its seeds (conkers) are rounder and shinier. Remember: yellow flowers = yellow buckeye, white flowers = horse-chestnut.
contextualKnowledge: Yellow buckeye is the state tree of Ohio, where it's much more common and grows naturally. In New England, any yellow buckeye you encounter is almost certainly a planted specimen rather than a wild native tree, as this species naturally occurs much further south and west.
compareHints: Yellow buckeye differs from the more common horse-chestnut by its yellow flowers (vs. white with pink spots) and generally smoother seed pods. Ohio buckeye, another relative, has similar yellow flowers but grows much smaller and has a more unpleasant odor when crushed. Red buckeye has similar leaves but bright red flowers and stays much shorter as a shrub or small tree.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Horse-chestnut is the only member of the Aesculus genus commonly found as a large tree in New England, making it fairly easy to distinguish from its relatives.
Unlike its tree-form relatives like horse-chestnut and Ohio buckeye, bottlebrush buckeye stays shrub-sized and spreads by suckers rather than growing as a single trunk.
Red buckeye is easily distinguished from other buckeyes by its bright red flowers - horse-chestnut has white flowers, Ohio buckeye has yellowish-green flowers, and yellow buckeye has yellow flowers.
Among buckeyes, Ohio buckeye is distinguished by having exactly 5 leaflets (not 7 like horse-chestnut) and yellowish-green flowers rather than the showy white or red flowers of other buckeye species.
